title: Show HN: Enso Method – agent skills for building software for someone else
text:
The Enso Method is a new set of AI skills for Claude Code and Codex which I've open sourced on GitHub predominantly for developers who build for someone else who is making the product/business calls.

I've been using AI to write basically 100% of my code since late 2024, back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, when it barely worked and there were few people doing this and very little support for this way of developing. I stubbornly thought this was going to be the future and came up with a methodology for making it work, before "AI skills" were even a thing. Since then I've continued to refine the method and I just recently published it as open source. The method focuses on requirements (PRD, TDD) up front, and has skills that autonomously refine the requirements, declaring assumptions that should be validated by stakeholders. It doesn't expect you to be a solo founder or that whoever is at the keyboard directing Claude or Codex to be the product owner and business decider in addition to being the developer. I think most of us sit in the seat where we develop for someone else who decides. And if AI is all about velocity, then if we have to slow down to get product owners to review and decide, that puts a serious damper on the efficiency everyone expects from AI development. So a defining attribute of the Enso Method is, when it reviews the requirements prior to implementation, it asks what questions/gaps there are and it tries to answer its own questions. If it can get to 95%+ confidence in the answers, it just rolls with those. If less then it will declare the assumption in an assumptions.md file which gets routed to business stakeholders to review. In the meantime however we still consider this to be a green light, we can move forward and implement with the assumptions, and if we later hear from the business that the assumption was wrong, we update the requirements and re-implement, because implementation is now cheap, and waiting isn't.

Fine tuning is a huge deal. I made some simple games and spent a lot of time on fine tuning little details about the movement trying to nail the right "feeling". The feeling of Mario's movement in Mario 64 is excellent. That feeling immediately makes the game fun even when just jumping around aimlessly.

It's very difficult to get right. Even with the exact same programming logic, tiny tweaks to certain numbers around velocity, acceleration, friction, impulse, etc all can have a huge impact on feel. So even without changing anything besides a single static value here or there you can make the game feel very different. (and then of course you can also add more logic and tweak things endlessly, like adding coyote time, jumping higher when you hold the button, nudging the player slightly into place instead of stopping flat if they are grazing an object... and then other things like sounds and animations can themselves completely change the feel without changing the systems at all)

Feel is also something that is very subjective. Some people might like something that feels very tight and responsive, some people might like something that feels more floaty or forgiving. A lot of people are aware of public key cryptography or asymmetric encryption, its already supported as identification & authentication method in sensitive places via MTLS. The whole idea of MTLS is about the server verifying the identity of the client and one of the core concepts is validating that the client certificate is issued by some Certificate Authority that can be trusted by the server. Its Phishing resistant, meaning some one cannot trick you into giving them the your credential that they can use by accident. The client certificates could be baked into physical devices (PIC, CAC cards) or Digital certificate on your machine. MTLS is used universally for machine to machine communication, however there is a certain degree of complexity so its not used everywhere for user identity.

1. FIDO is trying to leverage the same concept and trying to make it bit easier for use compared to MTLS. The core idea is to just use it for authentication not identification. It allows the user to authentication as long as the client can prove that they have the private key for a corresponding public key

2. Passkeys were/are target for Enterprise/Workforce users. When a consumer account is hacked the impacted user is just the consumer, whereas when an Employee account is hacked the entire company is at risk.

3. Passkeys/ (WebAuthn+CTAP) have been there for a while. Its still still evolving and everyone (platforms, Browsers, OS, Password managers, IDPs) wants to get something out of it which keeps on making it more complex

Since the client/authenticator is storing the private key, its important to ensure that they are doing it in a uniform and secure way. The authenticator implements a protocol called CTAP and they are supposed to conform to certain tests. The attestation is a means to ensure that the authenticator is doing the least minimum from security perspective.

Personally I do not like the idea of centralization, however as long as the path to attestation for different passkey providers is not locked I would say the attestation is a part of security.

At the same time the things I would worry about would be if the Authenticator provider starts generating a unique attestation for every user in customer identity space (its almost 0 cost in case of software based authenticators). A unique certificate for every authenticator instead of a batch one is where the privacy would be leaked, its akin to fingerprint. Some big companies are already doing it for their employees, thats a valid use case, employees unfortunately do not have a privacy when they are acting on behalf of the company

"Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary."

I think that's why FastCGI exists. It is the equivalent of PHP's "Swoole" or "FrankenPHP" or "amphp" or Laravel's "octane", etc. Each process is long-lived and tries to clean up its state as much as possible between requests. Forking a new process can take around 8ms (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19005586)

When I was building https://github.com/Qbix/webserver in PHP, I was faced with forking a new process per request. I implemented fork-per-request at first, similar to PHP-FPM and then implemented the "FastCGI" approach of long-lived processes that clean up after each request. (Modern PHP has introspection so the engine can know what to clean up, before calling the php files to handle things.) However, some things are not really possible to completely reset in PHP, and you have to be careful with database connection pools, etc. Typically those are left open even by preforking processes like php-fpm.

Anyway, I ended up flipping it: use the "FastCGI" approach as a default, and if the original PHP code doesn't work (rare), then for that app, you can choose the regular CGI approach of forking a process per request. That way you get maximum speed by default, and manually opt into safety (this is an exception to my usual priorities).

PHP is actually quite fast. But I was also interested in transpiling it to C. So I built the transpiler at: https://ulanguage.org/playground ... used Claude to transform about 1000 PHP functions to their native equivalents, but if you use any of the others, it would hook into the Zend runtime and link with it. (There are some nuances with zvals and objects, and resources in previous PHP versions, but I managed to overcome them.) By the way, it also works with Node and Python FFI the same way.

You can basically now take PHP, Python or Javascript/Typescript code, and speed up the CPU-bound parts about 10-50x. A lot of that is because of string and JSON handling. Many web apps use strings and JSON a lot. So underneath, I had the compiler use "ropes" for the strings, and avoid concatenation. It also parallelizes the JSON encode and decode into code that can run on multiple cores at once, i.e. large JSON payloads are encoded and decoded in parallel. Those are just huge speedups.

Anyway... all of this is mostly focused on speed optimization, so you can solve the literally C100K problem (forget C10K) today, on a regular box. If you don't need speed or FastCGI, your approach is fast enough for the vast majority of applications.
